title: A Cosmic Holiday Ornament, Hubble-Style
caption: Planetary nebula NGC 5189, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 5189 · constellation Musca · about 3,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A bright golden ring twists and tilts through the frame among bluish lobes of knotty, filament-laced gas. This is NGC 5189, a planetary nebula about 3,000 light-years away in the constellation Musca, whose intricate shape NASA likened to a glass-blown holiday ornament wrapped in a glowing ribbon.

A planetary nebula marks the last, short phase of life for a medium-sized star like the Sun. As the dying star burns the last fuel in its core, it throws off much of its outer envelope. Radiation from the remaining star heats that material until it glows, and because the star sheds mass unevenly in time and direction, the clouds take on complex shapes.

NGC 5189 has two nested structures, tilted relative to each other and expanding in different directions. A companion star orbiting the central star could explain this pattern, though no visible candidate has been found. The central remnant is now a white dwarf. The golden ring is made of radial filaments and cometary knots, usually shaped by ionizing radiation and stellar winds.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image. NASA shows F502N (oxygen) in cyan, F657N (hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen) in orange, F673N (sulfur) in green, F606W in blue and F814W in yellow.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of individual elements, and the colors are assigned to separate them rather than to match what an eye would see.

behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 recorded the nebula in filters tuned to the colors of glowing sulfur, hydrogen and oxygen atoms, while broad filters in visible and near-infrared light captured the colors of the stars. The total exposure time was 7 hours.
